summary: This informational document analyzes threats against Internet mail that signature-based mail authentication, especially DomainKeys Identified Mail, is meant to address. It discusses who the bad actors are, where they are, what they can do and what they hope to achieve.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a better lock for the mailbox, you think about who might sneak in and why. This describes the sneaky people who fake email and what they want.

subtitle: The security problems that signature-based email authentication was designed to prevent.

tldr.problem: Email is vulnerable to spoofing and abuse: attackers can send messages that appear to come from legitimate domains, enabling fraud, malware delivery, and reputation attacks. The mechanisms for such attacks are diverse and sophisticated.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4686 analyzes the threat landscape against email in detail: who the attackers are, where they operate, what they can do, and what they are trying to accomplish. This analysis informed the design of DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail), which uses cryptographic signatures to prove domain responsibility for messages.
tldr.outcome: The threat analysis enabled DKIM to be designed with clear knowledge of which attacks it prevents, which it mitigates partially, and which remain outside its scope—leading to more realistic expectations about email security.

today: RFC 4686 remains the authoritative threat analysis for email authentication. It has not been obsoleted and continues to inform DKIM deployment and expectations.

sections.title: Introduction and Threat Model
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) is a mechanism for cryptographically signing email messages to prove that a signing domain is responsible for a message. The recipient can verify the signature by retrieving the signer's public key from DNS and confirming the message was attested to by someone with the domain's private key.

RFC 4686 analyzes the threats that DKIM is intended to address, breaking them down into bad actors, their capabilities, their locations, and the bad acts they want to commit.

The document uses an "administrative unit" model. An administrative unit (AU) is a portion of the email path under common administration—typically the originating domain's infrastructure, intermediate relays, and the recipient's email system. Trust relationships develop between email systems and their administrative units to perform signing and verification.

DKIM operates entirely on message content (body and selected headers per RFC 2822), not on SMTP envelope information like the envelope-from address. This allows verification to work via protocols other than SMTP (POP, IMAP) and keeps DKIM scope clear and auditable.
sections.plainLanguage: Email is like postcards: anyone can write any sender address. DKIM is a way to make a tamper-proof signature on the card so the receiver knows it really came from the person who claims to have sent it.

sections.title: Bad Actors and Their Capabilities
sections.content:
RFC 4686 describes a spectrum of attackers with increasing sophistication and financial motivation.

Low-end: Simple attackers send unwanted email using commercially available tools, often falsifying the origin address. These may evolve to generating message signatures.

Mid-tier: "Professional" senders of unsolicited email deploy their own infrastructure: Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs), registered domains, and networks of compromised computers ("zombies") to send bulk messages and harvest email addresses. Often they operate as commercial enterprises and send on behalf of third parties.

High-end: Sophisticated, financially-motivated attackers stand to gain substantial benefit from email-based fraud. They employ the above mechanisms and additionally attack Internet infrastructure itself, including DNS cache poisoning and IP routing attacks.

All bad actors have access to extensive email corpora from target domains, knowledge of their business models, and access to public keys. They can submit messages to MTAs at multiple locations, construct arbitrary headers, sign messages for domains they control, generate unsigned or fake-signed messages for denial-of-service, replay previously signed messages, and transmit with any envelope information. The most sophisticated attackers can manipulate IP routing, poison DNS, control zombie networks for brute-force attacks, and eavesdrop on traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers range from kids using email tools to sophisticated criminals with stolen computer networks and deep pockets.

sections.title: Types of Email Abuse
sections.content:
The bad acts attackers attempt fall into several categories.

Use of arbitrary identities: Sending messages that obscure the real author, either the bad actor themselves or a compromised third-party computer. DKIM can help when coupled with Sender Signing Practices that state domains sign all their messages, making unsigned mail suspicious. DKIM alone cannot prevent abuse of addresses the attacker controls.

Use of specific identities: Impersonating particular legitimate domains. This includes exploiting social relationships (mimicking trusted senders), identity-related fraud (phishing, false invoices), reputation attacks (the "joe job"—harming a competitor's reputation by sending spam on their behalf), and reflection attacks (sending unsigned messages that bounce back to the target address as delivery failures).

Attacks on message signatures themselves: Includes theft of private keys, key recovery via side-channel attacks, replaying previously signed messages, denial-of-service against verifiers or key services, canonicalization abuse, body length limit abuse, compromised systems within originating domains, and cryptographic weaknesses.

Attacks on Sender Signing Practices: These declare whether a domain signs all its messages. Attackers can spoof SSP replies, create look-alike domain names, abuse internationalized domain names with similar characters, or use multiple from addresses to evade detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers fake where emails come from, steal signatures, replay old emails, and even fake the fingerprints that prove authenticity.

sections.title: Specific Attacks and Their Impact
sections.content:
RFC 4686 catalogs attacks with impact and likelihood ratings.

High-impact attacks affecting entire domains: Key theft, compromise of key servers, publication of malformed keys, cryptographic weaknesses, and compromised systems in the originating network.

Medium-impact attacks affecting specific users or periods: Delegated key theft (when domain owners delegate signing to third parties), revoked key use, falsified key service replies, display name abuse, verification probe attacks, and body length limit abuse.

Low-impact attacks affecting isolated messages: Chosen message replay (getting the target domain to sign a malicious message, then resending it), and canonicalization abuse (modifying message content while maintaining valid signatures).

High-likelihood attacks: Display name abuse, signed message replay, and denial-of-service attacks are expected frequently or continually.

Medium-likelihood attacks: Chosen message replay, canonicalization abuse, and various key compromises occur occasionally or affect some users frequently.

Low-likelihood attacks: Theft of domain-level keys, side-channel key recovery, and domain-level key server compromise are rare.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attacks are easy and happen all the time; others are hard and rare. DKIM helps stop some, makes others harder, and cannot stop things inside the originating domain or domain spoofing with look-alike names.

sections.title: What DKIM Does and Does Not Prevent
sections.content:
The RFC makes clear DKIM's scope: it is designed for externally-located bad actors outside the administrative units of the originating and receiving domains. Within these units, other mechanisms like authenticated message submission are more practical.

DKIM proves that a domain attested to a message. It does not prevent abuse of addresses controlled by bad actors. A valid signature proves someone with the domain's private key created it, not that the signer is legitimate. Reputation systems, whitelists, and accreditation are necessary complements.

DKIM cannot prevent attacks originating within the originating domain's administrative unit (rogue users, malware-infected systems) before the signature is applied. It cannot prevent attacks within the recipient's administrative unit. It cannot prevent spoofing of look-alike domain names or internationalized domain names with similar characters, though it can support reputation systems in detecting them. It does not validate SMTP envelope information, only message content.

DKIM is most effective when domains use Sender Signing Practices to advertise that they sign all messages, making unsigned messages from their domain obviously suspicious to verifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: DKIM proves a domain sent the email, but not whether they are good or bad. It stops outside attackers from faking domain signatures, but not people inside the domain, and not people with similar-looking domain names.
